questions.topicName: BOOM: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I
questions.stem: In this individual, dietary lactose is not cleaved at the intestinal brush border and instead reaches colonic bacteria. What mechanism most directly produces the resulting watery diarrhea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial invasion of the intestinal wall causing inflammation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of the intestinal epithelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Direct toxin-mediated activation of enterocyte chloride secretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unabsorbed lactose and its metabolites osmotically draw water

explanation.summary: Lactase deficiency leaves lactose undigested; bacterial fermentation yields gas and lactic acid, and the osmotically active undigested sugar plus metabolites pull water into the lumen, producing osmotic diarrhea, bloating and flatulence.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lactase deficiency leaves lactose undigested; bacterial fermentation yields gas and lactic acid, and the osmotically active undigested sugar plus metabolites pull water into the lumen, producing osmotic diarrhea, bloating and flatulence.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactose intolerance is a noninflammatory digestive defect; invasive bacteria cause bloody inflammatory diarrhea with fever, not post-dairy watery diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bile acid diarrhea follows terminal ileal disease or resection, not undigested lactose reaching the colon.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autoimmune epithelial injury describes celiac disease or autoimmune enteropathy; primary lactase deficiency involves an intact epithelium with low enzyme expression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxin-driven chloride secretion (cholera, ETEC) causes secretory diarrhea that persists with fasting; lactose diarrhea stops when the sugar is withheld.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I
questions.stem: An oxidizing agent acts on the open-chain form of glucose to yield the product shown at right. Which functional-group conversion has occurred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A hydroxyl is reduced to an aldehyde

choices.label: B
choices.text: A phosphate is esterified to C6

choices.label: C
choices.text: The C1 aldehyde is oxidized to a carboxylic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: The C6 alcohol is oxidized to a ketone

choices.label: E
choices.text: An amine is added to C2

explanation.summary: Oxidation of the exposed aldehyde carbonyl at C1 of glucose produces gluconate, a sugar acid; this reducing-sugar reaction underlies assays that detect glucose.
explanation.whyCorrect: Oxidation of the exposed aldehyde carbonyl at C1 of glucose produces gluconate, a sugar acid; this reducing-sugar reaction underlies assays that detect glucose.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Converting a hydroxyl to an aldehyde is an oxidation, not a reduction, and C1 of open-chain glucose is already an aldehyde.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Adding phosphate to a sugar is a kinase reaction, not oxidation, and would give glucose-6-phosphate rather than a sugar acid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: C6 is a primary alcohol; oxidizing it would give an aldehyde or a carboxylic acid (glucuronic acid), never a ketone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Adding an amine to C2 forms an amino sugar such as glucosamine; it is a transamination-type step, not oxidation.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I
questions.stem: Two forms of starch are shown: one is a linear chain and the other contains a periodic branch point. What is the functional consequence of the branching linkage that distinguishes amylopectin from amylose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It prevents the molecule from being stored intracellularly

choices.label: B
choices.text: It renders the polymer water-insoluble and structural

choices.label: C
choices.text: It converts the sugar units from glucose to galactose

choices.label: D
choices.text: It makes the polymer indigestible by human enzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: It creates additional non-reducing ends that speed enzymatic release of glucose

explanation.summary: Amylose is joined only by α-1,4 bonds, while amylopectin adds α-1,6 branch points. Each branch adds a non-reducing terminus, allowing amylases and phosphorylases to mobilize glucose from many ends simultaneously.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amylose is joined only by α-1,4 bonds, while amylopectin adds α-1,6 branch points. Each branch adds a non-reducing terminus, allowing amylases and phosphorylases to mobilize glucose from many ends simultaneously.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amylopectin is the main form of starch stored in plant granules; branching aids storage rather than preventing it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Branching increases solubility and accessibility; insoluble structural polymers like cellulose are linear chains with β-1,4 bonds.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both forms of starch are made entirely of glucose; branching changes linkage type (α-1,6), not the identity of the monomer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Starch is readily digested by amylase, and isomaltase/sucrase-isomaltase cleaves the α-1,6 branch points.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I
questions.stem: This structural polysaccharide of plants is a linear glucose polymer joined by the linkage highlighted at right. Why can humans not derive energy from it despite its being pure glucose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is too highly branched for amylase to access

choices.label: B
choices.text: The glucose units are in the L-configuration and cannot be metabolized

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is covalently bound to protein and cannot be cleaved

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its glucose is permanently oxidized to gluconate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Humans lack an enzyme that can hydrolyze the β-1,4 glycosidic bond

explanation.summary: Cellulose uses β-1,4 linkages; human digestive enzymes (amylases) cleave only α-1,4 bonds, so cellulose passes through as indigestible dietary fiber.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cellulose uses β-1,4 linkages; human digestive enzymes (amylases) cleave only α-1,4 bonds, so cellulose passes through as indigestible dietary fiber.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cellulose is a linear, unbranched polymer; the problem is its β-1,4 linkage, not branching.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cellulose is built from D-glucose, the same sugar humans metabolize; only the β-configuration of the glycosidic bond differs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cellulose is a pure carbohydrate polymer and is not covalently attached to protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cellulose glucose units are not oxidized; once freed (as by microbial cellulases) they are ordinary glucose.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I
questions.stem: In this enterocyte, glucose is moved from the intestinal lumen across the apical membrane against its concentration gradient. What directly powers this uphill transport?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct ATP hydrolysis by the apical glucose carrier

choices.label: D
choices.text: GLUT-2 pumping glucose in from blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: Facilitated diffusion driven by glucose alone

explanation.summary: SGLT-1 is a secondary active symporter: it couples glucose uptake to Na+ flowing down the gradient set up by the Na+/K+ ATPase. Glucose then exits basolaterally by facilitated diffusion through GLUT-2.
explanation.whyCorrect: SGLT-1 is a secondary active symporter: it couples glucose uptake to Na+ flowing down the gradient set up by the Na+/K+ ATPase. Glucose then exits basolaterally by facilitated diffusion through GLUT-2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fructose enters through GLUT5 by facilitated diffusion and is not coupled to glucose transport, so its gradient cannot drive glucose uptake.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SGLT1 does not hydrolyze ATP itself; ATP is used indirectly by the basolateral Na+/K+ ATPase, making this secondary rather than primary active transport.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GLUT2 is on the basolateral membrane and moves glucose out of the enterocyte toward blood by facilitated diffusion, not into the cell from blood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Facilitated diffusion can only move glucose down its gradient; uptake against the gradient requires coupling to Na+ influx.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I
questions.stem: Glucose and fructose are compared here. They share the molecular formula C6H12O6 but differ in the position of their carbonyl group. What is their structural relationship?

choices.label: D
choices.text: They are identical molecules in different conformations

explanation.summary: Both are hexoses with formula C6H12O6, but glucose carries an aldehyde at C1 and fructose a ketone at C2. Different connectivity of the same atoms makes them constitutional isomers.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both are hexoses with formula C6H12O6, but glucose carries an aldehyde at C1 and fructose a ketone at C2. Different connectivity of the same atoms makes them constitutional isomers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anomers differ only at the anomeric carbon of a cyclized sugar (α vs β), whereas glucose and fructose differ in the position of the carbonyl itself.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images, such as D- and L-glucose, with identical connectivity; glucose and fructose have different connectivity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Conformations interconvert by bond rotation alone; changing an aldehyde at C1 to a ketone at C2 changes bonding, so they are distinct molecules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Epimers are stereoisomers differing at one chiral carbon, such as glucose and galactose at C4; aldose versus ketose is a structural difference.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I
questions.stem: The open-chain sugars at top spontaneously convert to the ring forms at bottom. What type of intramolecular reaction produces these cyclic structures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dehydration to form a double bond

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oxidation of the carbonyl to a carboxylic acid

explanation.summary: An internal hydroxyl (C5 for glucose, C5 for fructose) attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a cyclic hemiacetal (aldose) or hemiketal (ketose); this creates the new anomeric center marked with an asterisk.
explanation.whyCorrect: An internal hydroxyl (C5 for glucose, C5 for fructose) attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming a cyclic hemiacetal (aldose) or hemiketal (ketose); this creates the new anomeric center marked with an asterisk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cyclization adds a hydroxyl across the carbonyl without losing water; no carbon-carbon double bond is formed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ring closure involves no change in oxidation state; oxidation of the aldehyde to a carboxylic acid would give gluconic acid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peptide bonds join an amine to a carboxyl group in proteins; sugars cyclize by hydroxyl attack on the carbonyl.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Esters form between a carboxylic acid and an alcohol; joining two hydroxyls would form an ether, and neither occurs in ring closure.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I
questions.stem: Three common disaccharides are shown. One of them cannot act as a reducing sugar because both anomeric carbons are tied up in its glycosidic bond. Which one is it?

explanation.summary: Sucrose links glucose C1 to fructose C2 (α-1,2), engaging both anomeric carbons, so it has no free reducing end. Lactose and maltose each retain a free anomeric carbon and are reducing sugars.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sucrose links glucose C1 to fructose C2 (α-1,2), engaging both anomeric carbons, so it has no free reducing end. Lactose and maltose each retain a free anomeric carbon and are reducing sugars.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cellobiose is a glucose β-1,4 dimer whose second glucose keeps a free anomeric carbon, so it is a reducing sugar.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Maltose links glucose units α-1,4, leaving the second glucose's anomeric carbon free, so it reduces Benedict reagent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Isomaltose links glucose units α-1,6, leaving one anomeric carbon free, so it is a reducing sugar.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lactose joins galactose C1 to glucose C4 (β-1,4), so the glucose's anomeric carbon is free and lactose is a reducing sugar.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I
questions.stem: The open-chain glucose cyclizes into the two ring forms shown, which differ only in the orientation of the hydroxyl at the newly formed stereocenter, C1 (the former carbonyl carbon). What are these two interconverting forms called?

explanation.summary: Ring closure creates a new stereocenter at C1 (the anomeric carbon); the α and β forms differ only in the configuration at that single carbon and are therefore anomers that interconvert by mutarotation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ring closure creates a new stereocenter at C1 (the anomeric carbon); the α and β forms differ only in the configuration at that single carbon and are therefore anomers that interconvert by mutarotation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Constitutional isomers differ in atom connectivity, like glucose and fructose; α and β glucose share connectivity and differ only in configuration at C1.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aldoses and ketoses differ in carbonyl type; both ring forms here come from the same aldose, glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epimers differ at a single chiral carbon other than the anomeric one, such as glucose versus galactose at C4; a difference at C1 after cyclization defines anomers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Enantiomers are mirror images differing at every chiral center (D- vs L-glucose); the α and β forms differ at only one carbon.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I
questions.stem: This disaccharide joins a six-membered pyranose ring to a five-membered furanose ring through their two anomeric carbons. Which sugar is depicted?

explanation.summary: The molecule is a glucopyranose linked to a fructofuranose via an α-1,2 glycosidic bond joining both anomeric carbons, the defining structure of sucrose (table sugar).
explanation.whyCorrect: The molecule is a glucopyranose linked to a fructofuranose via an α-1,2 glycosidic bond joining both anomeric carbons, the defining structure of sucrose (table sugar).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Maltose is two glucopyranose rings linked α-1,4, with no furanose ring and a free anomeric carbon.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Trehalose links both anomeric carbons, but joins two glucopyranoses (α-1,1); it has no five-membered fructofuranose ring.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cellobiose is two glucopyranoses linked β-1,4, with no furanose ring and a free reducing end.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lactose is galactopyranose linked β-1,4 to glucopyranose; both rings are six-membered and only one anomeric carbon is involved.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I
questions.stem: This highly branched storage polymer of glucose, found in animal liver and muscle, uses α-1,4 bonds along its chains and α-1,6 bonds at branch points roughly every 8-12 residues. What molecule is shown?

explanation.summary: The dense branching pattern with α-1,4 chains, α-1,6 branch points, numerous non-reducing ends, and a reducing end attached to the primer protein glycogenin identifies mammalian glycogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The dense branching pattern with α-1,4 chains, α-1,6 branch points, numerous non-reducing ends, and a reducing end attached to the primer protein glycogenin identifies mammalian glycogen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amylopectin is plant starch; it branches less often (about every 24-30 residues) and is not found in animal liver and muscle.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Amylose is an unbranched α-1,4 glucose chain from plant starch with no α-1,6 branch points.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cellulose is an unbranched β-1,4 glucose polymer forming plant cell walls, not an animal storage fuel.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Dextran is a bacterial and yeast glucose polymer built mainly on α-1,6 linkages, not mammalian storage glycogen.

questions.topicName: BOOM: Carbohydrates and Carbohydrate Metabolism Overview I
questions.stem: In this pathway, when galactose is present in excess the aldose reductase branch generates a poorly-metabolized sugar alcohol that accumulates. In which tissue does this accumulation most classically cause disease?

explanation.summary: The high-Km aldose reductase pathway becomes active when galactose accumulates, converting it to galactitol. Galactitol is osmotically trapped in the lens, drawing in water and producing cataracts, a hallmark of galactokinase deficiency and classic galactosemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The high-Km aldose reductase pathway becomes active when galactose accumulates, converting it to galactitol. Galactitol is osmotically trapped in the lens, drawing in water and producing cataracts, a hallmark of galactokinase deficiency and classic galactosemia.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Galactosemia does cause liver injury, but through galactose-1-phosphate toxicity in hepatocytes, not osmotic galactitol in sinusoids; the classic galactitol lesion is cataract.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Skeletal muscle is not the classic site of galactitol injury; the osmotic damage characteristically appears in the lens.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Renal tubular dysfunction can occur in galactosemia, but galactitol trapping by aldose reductase classically causes lens cataracts.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cardiac myocytes are not a recognized target of galactitol accumulation; galactitol's hallmark effect is osmotic cataract.
